slides.title: Predicting river floods with AI
say: On 1 September 2006, when tropical storm Ernesto passed, the Northeast Cape Fear river rose above its high-flow level. The evening before, our LSTM gave no warning.
Our question: can an LSTM forecast river flow 1 to 3 days ahead better than simple models, and could its warnings be trusted?
The short answer: with a river gauge, the LSTM and the best simple model show no clear difference; for the warnings that matter, NOT YET.
We can say why: among the models tried, the limit is the information in the inputs, not the network.

To be plain: Claude Code wrote the code and ran the experiments under the team lead’s direction; independent AI reviewers checked the engine and the experiments. The team’s own checks are not yet done.

slides.title: The 12 basins were chosen by rule, not by hand: four in each of three landscapes, 34 years of daily data
say: The data set is CAMELS-US: 671 US basins with daily weather and river flow.
A rule chose our 12: four in each of three landscapes, with no missing day in 34 years. No flow statistic and no model score enters the rule.
Why an LSTM? A river remembers past rain, and an LSTM is a network with a memory.
Our score is the NSE: 1 is a perfect forecast, 0 is no better than always forecasting the average flow.
slides.handover: First: can the test be trusted?

slides.title: The test is fair: the test years chose no setting, and a check on made-up data found no leak from later days
say: Each period has one job: the training years fit the models, the validation years choose the settings, and the test years are only scored.
The models get four sets of inputs: past weather, with or without the river gauge, and each again with a perfect weather forecast.
The perfect weather forecast is an upper bound that cannot be had in practice.
A check on made-up rivers with a known answer found no leak.
Three independent AI reviewer agents tried to break the shared code. The team’s own check, which the plan gives to GNSS member 1, is not yet done.

slides.title: The number to beat comes from simple models: median NSE 0.56, 0.33 and 0.25 for 1, 2 and 3 days ahead with a river gauge
say: ‘Tomorrow = today’ repeats today’s flow; ridge regression and random forest are fitted on hand-made weather features.
With the river gauge they set the number to beat: a median NSE of 0.56 1 day ahead and 0.25 3 days ahead.
For warnings the honest test is the onset: a high-flow day forecast while the river was still below the high-flow level.
No simple model warns of more than 18% of the onsets.
slides.handover: That is the number to beat. Does the LSTM beat it?

slides.title: With a river gauge, the LSTM and the best simple model show no clear difference: milestone 2 is not met there
say: One LSTM for all 12 rivers, trained three times from different random starts; the forecasts are averaged.
With past weather and the river gauge, 1 day ahead, its median NSE is 0.59; the best simple model reaches 0.56. The numbers for 2 and 3 days ahead are on the slide.
The LSTM is higher in 5, 5 and 9 of 12 basins: no clear difference. With the river gauge, milestone 2 of our plan is not met.
With past weather only, the average of three trainings is ahead; a single training is not clearly ahead.
A Transformer shows no clear difference, and takes roughly 10 to 15 times as long. What does change the forecast?

slides.title: One onset, day by day: the same LSTM gives no warning with the river gauge and a warning with the upper bound
slides.figure_part: the part without the title and the footnote
say: Here is that event: Northeast Cape Fear, North Carolina, September 2006.
Black is the observed river flow; blue are the forecasts made the evening before.
On 1 September the river crosses the high-flow level: the onset. The LSTM with the river gauge gives no warning.
The same LSTM, given a perfect weather forecast, does. That is an upper bound that cannot be had in practice.
Same network, more information: 179 mm of rain are stamped on the onset day, so they were not yet in the model’s inputs.
The example was picked by rule; 308 of the 611 onsets went this way.
slides.handover: One event is not a score. How often does a warning come?

slides.title: Warnings: CAUTION for high-flow days 1 day ahead with a river gauge, NOT YET for onsets, the warnings that matter
say: The criteria were fixed before the analysis: GO needs at least 70% of high-flow days warned and at most 30% false warnings.
With the river gauge, 1 day ahead, the LSTM warns of 62% of the high-flow days: CAUTION.
But ‘tomorrow = today’ gets the same verdict: most high-flow days come when the river is already high.
For onsets, the warnings that matter, the verdict is NOT YET at 1, 2 and 3 days ahead: 1 day ahead, 81% of the onsets get no warning.
Only the upper bound, the same LSTM given a perfect weather forecast, reaches GO.
slides.handover: So why are the onsets missed?

slides.title: Onset warnings fail when the rain behind the rise is not yet in the model’s inputs
say: Look at the right-hand group: 335 of the 611 onsets.
There, most of the two days’ rain is stamped on the target day, so it was not yet in the model’s inputs.
The LSTM warns of 2% of them. In the left-hand group, where most of the rain is already in its inputs, it warns of 71%.
Careful: not yet in the inputs does not mean not yet fallen.
So when did that rain fall?
slides.if_late: Onsets are missed where the rain behind the rise is not yet in the inputs: 2% are warned there, against 71% where most of the rain is in. Not yet in the inputs does not mean not yet fallen; the details are in the report, section 5.

slides.title: 1 day ahead, rain stamped up to the evening of the issue day closes about a quarter of the gap in onsets warned; NSE: mixed
say: The data indicate that our rain table’s day ends in the morning, at about 09:00. That is an inference from our own data.
When a forecast is made in the evening, the rain since the morning has fallen but is not yet in the model’s inputs.

The test adds rain stamped up to the evening of the issue day. With the river gauge, 1 day ahead, onsets warned go from 19% to 30%; the control, the same rain one day older, gives 19%; the upper bound is 64%.
That is about a quarter of the gap. In NSE the result is mixed: the median rises, but only 5 of 12 basins gain.
The hours after about 17:30 are in neither model: next slide.

slides.title: Given the rain up to the issue time, onsets warned 1 day ahead go from 19% to 51%, or 48% with the real-time radar product in its place
slides.figure_part: the two panels with the names of the rungs and the legend, without the title and the footnote
say: ERA5 model rain to midnight warns of 30%, the same as NLDAS.
AORC, an analysis made after the fact, takes the onsets from 19% to 51%, hindsight at most about 3 points, and the median NSE from 0.59 to 0.77.
The control, the same rain over the table’s own window, gives 18%: the hours after 09:00 are worth 33.6 points.
Stage IV radar, the real-time product, in AORC’s place gives 48%, 45% without its last hour: a check on the test years, not a service.
The simple models gain as many onsets: the information, not the network. In NSE the LSTM gains about twice as much.
Onsets stay NOT YET: about half of the warnings are false.
slides.handover: That rain has fallen. What about the rain still to come?

slides.title: A real weather forecast lifts the onsets warned 2 and 3 days ahead from 8% and 6% (rain table alone) to 39% and 37%: still NOT YET
slides.figure_part: the columns for 2 and 3 days ahead, without the title, the legend and the footnote
say: A real forecast, one GEFS member, lifts the onsets warned 2 and 3 days ahead from 8% and 6%, with the rain table alone, to 39% and 37%.
In NSE the forecast lowers the 1-day score and the gains at 2 and 3 days are mixed: the 1-day median goes from 0.77 to 0.69.
1 day ahead, for the warnings, it is a moved operating point, not lost skill: fewer onsets, far fewer false warnings.
Onsets are still NOT YET.
slides.handover: So what did it take, and what is missing?

slides.title: The finding holds in both directions: taking information away lowered the skill, giving it raised it
say: Taking information away lowered the skill; giving it raised it.
It took two inputs: the rain up to midnight, and a weather forecast.

Still missing: about half of the onset warnings are false, so onsets are still NOT YET. Also missing: the other ensemble members, a network trained on the real-time product, and five trainings instead of three where NSE decides.
Limits: 12 basins, 9 test years, one laptop. The team’s own checks are not yet done.

slides.title: Among the models tried, the limit is the information in the inputs, not the network
say: Large marks: the LSTM; small marks: other models, close to it.
1 day ahead, with more information, the onsets warned rise from 19% to 30%, 51% (hindsight at most about 3 points) and 64%.
The last is an upper bound that cannot be had in practice. The diamonds, 48% and 45%, put real-time radar in AORC’s place: a check, not a service.
2 and 3 days ahead, a real forecast lifts them from 8% and 6% (rain table alone) to 39% and 37%.
So with the inputs that can be had in practice, changing the kind of model changed little; giving a model more information changed a lot.
Among the models tried, the limit is the information in the inputs, not the network.
Thank you. We welcome your questions.

slides.title: Learning curves: on one river the validation score peaks at update 50 and then falls; on 12 rivers it peaks at updates 500 to 800
say: These are the learning curves. Grey is the training loss, blue the NSE in the validation years.
On one river the validation score peaks at update 50 and then falls, while the training loss falls further: the network memorises its training years.
On 12 rivers the peak comes at updates 500 to 800. Early stopping keeps the state at the peak.

slides.title: A river remembers past rain: without a river gauge, weather older than 30 days still improves the forecast
say: A river remembers: its flow today depends on the rain of the past days to months.
An LSTM reads the days one after another and carries a memory from day to day.
On one river, 1 day ahead, the NSE is 0.12 with 2 days of past weather, 0.30 with 30 days and 0.36 with 365 days.

slides.title: A river never seen in training: the typical basin loses 0.13 NSE 1 day ahead; the median falls from 0.43 to 0.22
say: This is every basin 1 day ahead: the filled dot with the basin in training, the diamond with the basin held out.
A river never seen is harder: the typical basin loses 0.13 NSE 1 day ahead; the median falls from 0.43 to 0.22.
It is lower in 11 of 12 basins.

slides.title: More training rivers: no clear difference for the 12 rivers with a gauge 1 day ahead, but a river never seen gains: median NSE 0.22 → 0.38
slides.figure_part: the four panels with the legend, without the title and the footnote
say: We trained on 63 rivers instead of 12.
For the same 12 rivers with a gauge, 1 day ahead, the median NSE goes from 0.59 to 0.60: no clear difference.
A river never seen gains: from 0.22 to 0.38 with basin properties, and from 0.31 to 0.43 without them.
But the number, the variety and the nearness of the training rivers changed together, so scale and nearness are not separated.

slides.title: Warning scores 1 to 3 days ahead: the share warned and the share of warnings that were false
say: The top row is all high-flow days, the bottom row the onsets; left the share warned, right the share of warnings that were false.
The green bands are what GO asks for. With the river gauge, 1 day ahead, 19% of the onsets are warned.
The dashed line is the same LSTM given a perfect weather forecast. That is an upper bound that cannot be had in practice.

slides.title: A Transformer is not better here, and training it takes roughly 10 to 15 times as long
say: A Transformer was trained with the same data, trainer and test.
In the test years: no clear difference. The mean NSE is 0.401 for the LSTM and 0.402 for the Transformer.
Training it took roughly 10 to 15 times as long.
This holds for this data size, not for Transformers in general.
So with the inputs that can be had in practice, changing the kind of model changed little.

slides.title: Satellite rain lifts the forecast with a river gauge 1 and 2 days ahead: probably a later time stamp, not better rain
say: Satellite rain agrees only moderately with our rain table: the correlation is 0.59.
Yet with the river gauge it raises the median NSE from 0.54 to 0.61 1 day ahead.
The likely reason is the time stamp: its day ends in the evening of the issue day.
Water vapour can be derived from the delay of GNSS signals. We tested water vapour from a reanalysis, a weather model: no clear change in NSE. Real GNSS-derived vapour was not tested.
slides.if_late: Satellite rain points the same way, probably because of its later time stamp; the details are in the report, section 6.2.

late_cut.say: Onsets are missed where the rain behind the rise is not yet in the inputs: 2% are warned there, against 71% where most of the rain is in. Not yet in the inputs does not mean not yet fallen; the details are in the report, section 5.
